title: JSON vs SQL
explain: My rule of thumb: a JSONB document has better data locality because it replaces several SQL queries with one lookup. I embed data that is bounded, owned by its parent and read together, and I normalize data that is shared, unbounded or updated independently.
model:
Normalized order: rows in `orders`, `order_lines`, `products`; reading one order with everything means several lookups or joins touching different pages. Document order: the order and its lines sit together in one row, so one primary-key lookup returns all of it.

| Embed in JSONB when the data is... | Normalize into tables when the data is... |
| --- | --- |
| read together with the parent | **shared** across parents (a product in thousands of orders) |
| **owned** by the parent (order lines, address, settings) | **unbounded** (all followers, all events of a device) |
| **bounded** in size (a few to a few hundred items) | updated independently |
| rarely updated alone; shape changes fast | needs constraints, foreign keys, joins, aggregates |

**Costs of embedding:** a change to a shared fact must be rewritten everywhere it is embedded; a one-field update rewrites the whole document; the database cannot enforce foreign keys or NOT NULL inside it; cross-document aggregates are awkward.

Embedding can be *right*: an order should snapshot the unit price at purchase time. Keep the real join keys (order id, customer id, status) as columns. This is [data locality](#/sd/f/data-locality) applied to storage and an instance of [scalable simplicity](#/sd/f/scalable-simplicity).

details.q: Where should an order's 1 to 20 line items live?
details.a: Embedded in the order's JSONB document. They are bounded, owned and read together, so one lookup per order gives better locality at no loss. Keep order id, customer id and status as real columns for querying.

details.q: A user document embeds the follower list and one celebrity has 40 million followers. What breaks?
details.a: The document is unbounded, so every read and nearly every follow rewrites a huge value. Model followers as a separate relation (user_id, follower_id), which also supports the reverse query "who does X follow".

details.q: A product name is embedded in 40,000 orders of 4 KB each. What does fixing the name cost?
details.a: Rewriting every document: 40,000 x 4 KB = 160 MB plus index and WAL overhead, versus one row in a normalized `products` table. For historical facts like orders you usually keep the old name as a snapshot, which is why embedding mutable shared facts is the costly case.

details.q: What do you lose by using JSONB instead of columns?
details.a: Database-enforced foreign keys and NOT NULL inside the document, cheap single-field updates (the whole value is typically rewritten), and easy cross-document aggregation such as revenue per category. Those are why shared, constrained or analysed fields stay relational.

details.q: Can you still query inside JSONB?
details.a: Yes, with GIN or expression indexes, but you get weaker statistics and constraints than with columns. Promote fields you filter or join on to real columns.

details.q: How does this relate to a first design for a new product?
details.a: Start with documents for owned, read-together data and keep the join keys real; normalize later where a shared or unbounded relationship appears. That is the scalable-simplicity stance: simple now, with a clear migration path.

prompts.q: Explain the JSONB versus normalized-tables decision in terms of data locality.
points: One document row replaces multiple queries or joins
Normalize shared, unbounded or independently updated data

prompts.q: List the costs of denormalized copies and when embedding is still correct.
points: Shared facts must be rewritten wherever embedded
One-field updates rewrite the whole document
No database-level constraints inside the document
Snapshots like purchase-time price are correct to embed

prompts.q: Model a social app's users, posts and followers: say what you embed and what you keep relational.
points: Profile settings and small owned data embedded
Followers as a relation, since unbounded and queried both ways
Posts separate if they are many and independently updated
Real columns for keys used to query and join
